Summary: might be fun for a few hours with friends, but gets boring solo quickly. I got this because Iron Pineapple had so much fun with it. It really feels like a fun mod for Terraria, rather than a full blown game. The video tutorials are funny and charming and serve the purpose to get you into a mood where you don't take the game seriously, but the tutorial doesn't show you anything, especially the grapple hook jump. The game definitely feels like it's balanced around co-op, since defending 2 sides solo is a bit of a hassle. The economy feels unbalanced, as defenses can get destroyed easily (esp. solo, esp. when the game doesn't tell you that next wave will be a boss) and you decide whether to invest in defensive structures or leveling up your character. The game lacks variety in enemies and weapons, making runs feel similar.

BALANCING THESE WEAPONS AROUND IT MAKES ALMOST ALL OF THEM TRASH. - there's basically no build variety, almost all of the items are stat sticks also some issues unique to bonelords: - building is underpowered. you need support structures and most of it will come crumbling down pretty quickly once the actually threatening enemies show up - it's ugly as sin - the music is okay at its best if you see this game 50% off honestly it's worth it for the wizard tutorial alone, and also how good the best weapons feel to use, otherwise don't bother tbh

It's been a while since I played this, so I decided to remake the review. Bonelords is a game that attempts to fuse the combat of Dark Souls with the gameplay style of Terraria while also combining it with a Rogue-lite. Defend the fortress, defeat your enemies and get their bones. You can use all of it to buy blocks and traps or use it to level up your character. Let's start with the positives first. The music is pretty good, specially the boss themes. Genuinely recommend taking a listen to it on their Youtube channel, or by buying the soundtrack. This game has a pretty neat gimmick when a run ends. When it does, you get rewarded with a bone marrow of your character, allowing you to carry some of the stats, a relic or even a weapon to any other run. Every class has a unique perk that can be acquired that way too. Not only does this make you not feel as bad when you lose a run since you still get a marrow, but it also gives a reason to play on harder difficulty because it gives better marrows there. The graphics are ... presentable. But it does have its charm when you include the silly wizards teaching you how to play the game. It feels like a random old Flash game that you would find in Kongregate or Armor Games. Now for the negatives, and sadly it does have a ton: The game does not have enough replayability due to lack of content. You will always go for the same weapon that your class is good at. There's not enough blocks, traps, enemies and bosses. And sadly, more bosses are unlikely to get added since the developer is asking for a specific amount of sales of the game for him to add more, which sadly is not going to happen since a lot more is needed. Half of the relics don't really do anything interesting nor impactful enough, a good chunk just increases your stats and does nothing more. There's 3 weapon types, Melee, Magic and Ranged. Melee is by far, the worse to play. Since this game calls itself "Terraria-like", let's compare to it. Have you ever wondered why most "Melee" weapons in Terraria shoot projectiles or have long reach? Because the game would feel way worse without it, thanks to every enemy doing contact damage. If you ever wanted to experience what it would be like if weapons didn't do that, Bonelords is here to show you that. Simply put, it doesn't work. You constantly take damage and knockback since you have to get so close, and you barely have any I-frames either, so you just bounce around like a ball when using those weapons. It has no crowd control so you get overwhelmed, the fort gets destroyed, and you lose the run. It becomes [b] even worse [/b] when you're playing on a harder difficulty or with any of the challenges enabled. It's also the most boring weapon, most of them are too similar to each other. Magic and Ranged have more variety, are way better, easier and safer to use. Half of the traps aren't worth using, those being Flingtraps and Mines. Flingtraps just launches enemies and takes too long to do that again, and Landmines deal too much damage and are a waste of bones to be used on normal enemies, and are not powerful enough to be used on bosses and mini-bosses. Despite the wizards teaching how to grapple, I don't see a single reason to use it. Grappling Is useless and overshadowed by Dashing. It's too awkward to use while costing the same amount of Stamina as Dashing. Dashing is just better, specially considering that there's the Trickster class that has a faster dash and it makes dashes cost half the amount to use. And since I just mentioned something useless, we also have the Mobility stat. I don't see a single reason to ever increase this stat. If you're going Melee you go for Strength, Magic increase Magica and Ranged uses Precision. If you're too frail, increase Vitality. Mobility just increases Stamina and Movement Speed. There's no reason to increase those, there's no class that focuses on this stat. I'm not trying to throw the developer under a bus here, but the quality of this game is a little ... questionable to say the least. For example, I have proof that the dev doesn't test his own game. When the Floor Is Lava challenge was added, which was early in october, players would take unavoidable damage from the lava since the final boss teleports you to it, and it was only fixed at the end of december of last year because I reported it to the dev. This is something that the dev himself easily would have noticed if he just bothered to get to the end of a single run. And in one of the first few patch notes, he admitted to let an AI mess with the code, which ended up causing a bug. Also, I highly doubt the game is beatable with all modifiers while on the hardest difficulty, specially if you're using melee. This isn't a Hades situation where this is mostly designed for you to heavily customize the experience, since Bonelords only has a harder difficulty and 3 modifiers. If you're wondering why I changed my review from positive to negative, well, it's because of the new update, which added the new "Cursed Relics" challenge. What the hell is this? This genuinely looks like an april fools joke or something. Enabling this makes every single relic you grab also have a random negative effect. It does give you an additional relic at the start of a run, at the cost of that one having 2 negative effects instead of 1. This isn't a bad idea on paper, in fact, I want more relics to have downsides, there's only 2 new ones in the game with an actual risk or downside to use, those being the All-Or-Nothing Coin Slag (chance of taking double damage) and the Meat Cube (flasks heal less). The problem here is that the ones from the challenge are extremely punishing, and some are downright nonsensical. We have things such as: -25% less damage; 15% chance to lose all your bones after each wave; Shops are 70% more expensive; Unavoidable damage from a status effect passively activating on your character; Quick time events that if you fail, you instantly die; Cannot walk or dash to the left; Immediately lose all your non-relic items; And my personal favorite: You lose your first relic, and the game crashes. Yes, I'm not kidding. The updates were going well, we got issues being fixed and more items being added. Who asked for this? This looks like an out of season april fools joke. Genuinely horrible addition that no one is gonna enable since it's a meme. Oh, and fun fact: according to the developer this is a major update, the first major update we got in this game, what a joke. I can tolerate bugs, those happen, but this? Something intentionally bad? Hell no. [h2] Conclusion: [/h2] I heard of this game thanks to a silly ad on Youtube. I bought it with no expectations and was surprised that the game isn't bad. Trying to get most of the achievements was fun. But the game feels like it's in more of an early access state, and the latest update just sucks. There is potential here, but not enough content, rough edges and dubious decisions. It's an ok game. There's a lot of better Rogue-lites and Souls-likes in the market, but at least this one is quite cheap and somewhat unique. 5/10 game. 🦴

Wish i could give a neutral recommendation, but I'm going to put it at a no rather than a yes. i have no comment to make on the art style because as the dev said it's his first time doing pixel art and i really really respect that he made all of the graphics for the game himself, i think its very nice for what it is. The game itself is pretty fun the first time you play it, but past that, runs all feel pretty samey - you shoot for the same weapons and same stuff every time for each of the classes. the combat and bosses don't feel amazing, and the base building is pretty unintuitive. also not a fan of the ai vtuber in the intro. getting more specific into the base building aspect of the game, the idea of building up your keep and almost building it as a tower defense type of game is really cool but its executed poorly. i'd love to see it expanded upon and improved further. despite the game marketed as being terraria-like, the only real similarity is the graphical style. theres no progressing weapon or armor upgrades through crafting, the only way to get weapon upgrades, blocks, and defenses for your base is by making purchases between waves and as drops from enemies with nearly no rhyme or reason. one of the positives i really enjoy, though, is the legacy system. very cool that your characters will pass down their best traits to your next characters. this game has a lot of good ideas and the dev is very clearly passionate about it and i really respect that, but anything past the first run just doesn't feel very fun. for a game that is designed around replayability, that's not grat, which is why i'd love a neutral review instead of a straight yes or no recommendation.

Bonelords is an ambitious indie roguelike that blends fast-paced combat, defensive strategy, and long-term progression into a chaotic but highly rewarding experience. Developed by Z0 Game Studios, the game refuses to limit itself to a single genre. Instead, it combines side-scrolling action, Souls-inspired mechanics, tower defense systems, and roguelike structure into something that feels unpredictable and constantly engaging. The central objective revolves around protecting Fort Platz from endless enemy assaults while building stronger characters and reinforcing defenses between increasingly difficult waves. What initially seems like a simple action game quickly reveals surprising depth through its combat systems, build variety, and strategic gameplay layers. One of the game’s strongest aspects is its combat system. Movement feels fast and responsive, and battles rely heavily on timing, positioning, and quick reactions. Dodging attacks at the correct moment grants invulnerability frames, enemy attacks can be interrupted or deflected, and managing stamina during combat becomes essential during more difficult encounters. Every weapon type feels distinct, with different attack speeds, special abilities, and combat styles encouraging experimentation. The combat takes noticeable inspiration from Souls-like games, but it adapts those mechanics into a faster side-scrolling format that feels both challenging and satisfying. Character progression is another area where Bonelords excels. Players can choose from multiple starting classes, each offering different strengths and gameplay approaches. Some focus on aggressive melee combat, while others emphasize mobility, ranged attacks, or defensive utility. As runs continue, players gain access to relics, stat upgrades, and equipment combinations that significantly alter how combat unfolds. The flexibility of the build system encourages experimentation because nearly every run can evolve into something completely different depending on item choices and upgrade paths. What makes the game particularly interesting is how it combines direct combat with tower defense mechanics. Between waves, players can build walls, traps, and defensive structures to help protect the fortress from incoming enemies. These defenses are not simply passive additions; they require careful placement and strategic thinking to remain effective. Defensive structures can collapse under pressure, become damaged during fights, or even create dangerous situations if poorly positioned. This balance between personal combat skill and defensive planning gives the game a much deeper strategic layer than many standard roguelikes. The roguelike progression loop is also handled well through the game’s inheritance and legacy systems. Even failed runs contribute toward long-term advancement because players gradually unlock stronger traits, upgrades, and inherited bonuses for future characters. This system helps reduce frustration by ensuring that defeat still feels productive. Over time, players steadily gain access to stronger builds and more advanced strategies, creating a satisfying sense of progression across multiple attempts. Visually, Bonelords embraces a colorful and exaggerated art style filled with personality. Characters, monsters, and environments all carry a distinct indie charm that helps the game stand out from darker and more serious roguelikes. Enemy designs range from grotesque undead creatures to bizarre fantasy monsters, while bosses often combine intimidating attacks with humorous visual details. The side-scrolling perspective keeps the action readable even when the screen becomes filled with enemies, traps, and visual effects during chaotic later waves. The soundtrack and sound design contribute heavily to the game’s atmosphere. Music shifts naturally between calmer preparation phases and intense battle sequences, helping maintain momentum throughout each run. Combat sounds are especially satisfying, with impactful effects for weapon clashes, staggered enemies, collapsing walls, and powerful attacks making every fight feel energetic and dangerous. Cooperative multiplayer adds another layer of replayability. Playing with friends through local split-screen or Remote Play Together creates some of the game’s best moments, especially when coordinating defenses and combining different builds during difficult waves. The chaotic nature of combat becomes even more entertaining with multiple players managing different roles, and the cooperative systems fit naturally within the game’s design. Despite its strengths, Bonelords is not without flaws. The large number of mechanics introduced early on can feel overwhelming for new players, particularly those unfamiliar with roguelikes or skill-based combat systems. Difficulty spikes can also become unforgiving during certain runs, especially if players fail to build effective defenses or receive poor upgrade combinations. Some later battles become visually crowded as enemies, projectiles, and environmental effects flood the screen, occasionally making combat harder to read. Even with these issues, the game’s creativity and ambition consistently outweigh its rough edges. Bonelords succeeds because it fully commits to blending multiple genres instead of relying on a single gameplay formula. Every run feels unpredictable due to the variety of upgrades, enemy encounters, and defensive strategies available. The combination of strategic planning, fast action combat, and roguelike progression creates a gameplay loop that remains highly addictive over long sessions. For players who enjoy challenging roguelikes, tactical defense mechanics, and build-focused progression systems, Bonelords offers a deeply entertaining indie experience filled with replay value and personality. Its fusion of action-heavy combat and strategic fortification mechanics gives it a unique identity that separates it from many traditional roguelikes. While its steep learning curve and chaotic difficulty may not appeal to every player, those willing to master its systems will discover a rewarding and highly replayable game packed with creativity and satisfying progression. Rating: 8/10
